title: The flash sale on one partition
outcome: One seller's flash sale, keyed by seller ID, put 80% of the traffic on one partition, and more partitions changed nothing.

content.bookmark: A key always hashes to one partition. If one key carries most of the traffic, one partition and one consumer carry it, however many partitions there are.

check.prompt: Lag is high on one partition and near zero on the others. What is the likely cause?
options: Too few consumers in the group
A skewed key: one key sends far more records than the rest
check.why: Lag on one partition only, with one consumer saturated and the rest idle, is the classic sign of a hot key.

check.prompt: The topic is keyed by seller ID and one seller is hot. You double the partitions. What happens to that seller's records?
options: They still all go to one partition
check.why: The same key hashes to one partition whatever the count. More partitions add room for other keys, not for this one.

check.prompt: You change the key to seller ID plus a bucket number 0 to 3. What do you give up?
options: Ordering across that seller's records: order holds only within each bucket
check.why: Bucketing spreads the seller over up to four partitions. Order now holds within each bucket, not across all of the seller's records.

check.prompt: What does the producer do with a record that has no key?
options: Sends it to a sticky partition that changes after about a batch, spreading load
check.why: With no key the built-in partitioner sticks to a partition until at least batch.size bytes have gone, then moves on, which spreads load well. It gives no per-entity order.

caseStudy.setting: An online marketplace (fictional) publishes order events to marketplace.orders, keyed by seller ID, so each seller's orders are processed in order. A fulfilment group of 12 consumers reads 12 partitions and books couriers.

events.what: One large seller starts a flash sale. Within minutes, about 80% of all orders are theirs.
Lag on partition 7 climbs into the tens of thousands. The other 11 partitions are near zero. Couriers for the sale's orders are booked hours late.
The team raises the topic to 24 partitions and adds consumers. Partition 7's backlog doesn't move.

pipeline: Fulfilment group · one consumer per partition, books a courier per order
Courier API · called once per order
tasks: Why did adding partitions not help?
Does anything really need all of one seller's orders in order?

debrief.title: Why more partitions didn't help
text: Every record with that seller's ID hashes to the same partition, so one partition, and the single consumer that owns it, received 80% of the traffic.
Adding partitions gave other keys more room. The hot key stayed on one partition, and the change also moved other sellers' keys (scenario 4).

debrief.title: Choosing the key from what needs order
text: Booking a courier needs each order's own events in order, not every order of one seller. Keying by order ID spreads the sale evenly and keeps what matters in order.
Ask of any key: what is the smallest thing whose events must be applied in sequence? That is the key.

debrief.title: If the key really must stay
text: Bucket it: seller ID plus a bucket number. Load spreads over several partitions, and order holds only within each bucket.
Or route the known heavy seller to its own topic with its own consumers.
Watch for skew before it bites: per-partition bytes in, and lag per partition, not just total lag.

takeaway: One key, one partition, one consumer.
Key by the smallest thing that needs order.
More partitions can't split a hot key.
content.honesty: If you haven't dealt with a hot partition, say so and explain the reasoning. If you have, lead with how you found it and what it cost.

tasks: What business rule decides the key?
What would you specify for large sellers' events?

debrief.title: The business rule
text: "Which events must be handled in order?" Here: each order's own events, not each seller's.
That answer, from the business, decides the key.

debrief.title: Specifying for large sellers
text: Fulfilment time stays within target during a sale by the largest seller; tested with a simulated flash sale.

sayIt.question: How would you help a team choose what to key events by?
points: Ask what must happen in order, in business terms.
Key by the smallest entity that needs order.
Ask about the biggest key: a large customer, a default value.
Know that more partitions don't fix a hot key.
Ask for a test with the largest realistic key.

tasks: What is the impact on the seller and their customers?
How do you plan for large sellers' events?

debrief.title: Impact
text: Late couriers for the platform's biggest seller during its biggest event; talk to the seller directly.

debrief.title: Planning
text: Ask large sellers to share sale plans, and test the platform against their expected peak.

sayIt.question: Your biggest customer's peak overloaded one part of the system. How do you respond?
points: Talk to the customer directly about impact.
Explain the cause simply: all their traffic went through one lane.
Fund the fix: a better key, or a dedicated path.
Plan with large customers before their peaks.
Test with the largest realistic customer.

tasks: What do you do during the sale?
What do you change for next time?

debrief.title: During the sale
text: Stop changing partitions. Speed up the one hot consumer if possible, and tell the seller about delays.

debrief.title: Next time
text: Add per-partition lag to dashboards; a known-sale calendar with load tests before each.

sayIt.question: How would you handle a hot partition during a live event?
points: Recognise it: lag on one partition, one busy consumer.
Don't add partitions mid-event; it doesn't help and moves keys.
Contain impact and communicate.
Plan the real fix after: the key.
Add per-partition monitoring.

tasks: What key would you choose, and why?
How would you detect skew early?

debrief.title: The key
text: Order ID: courier booking needs each order's events in order, and order IDs spread evenly.
If per-seller order were required, bucket the seller ID, accepting order only within each bucket.

debrief.title: Detecting skew
text: Dashboards of bytes in and lag per partition, with an alert when one partition exceeds the median by a set factor.

sayIt.question: What is a hot partition, and how would you fix one?
points: One partition gets far more traffic, usually from a skewed key.
Signs: lag on one partition, one consumer saturated.
More partitions don't help; the key always hashes to one.
Fix by choosing a finer key, bucketing the key, or isolating the heavy key.
Each fix trades away some ordering; say which.
